paper.title: RISED: RubrIcs for agentic multi-environment Selection and sElf-Distillation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Training a single LLM agent jointly across diverse interactive environments has attracted increasing attention as a route to generalist agents. Existing curriculum and data-selection strategies often allocate training at the environment level or prioritize local reward-based signals, without explicitly considering relationships between current rollouts across environments for prompt-group selection. Meanwhile, as environments are learned at different rates, all-failure and all-success rollout groups can coexist within a batch, leaving those data without group-relative reward signals. Both challenges highlight limitations of relying solely on scalar rewards in multi-environment RL: they provide limited information about cross-environment relationships and no within-group reward contrast when rewards are identical. This motivates richer textual feedback, such as rubrics describing rollout behaviours, to guide learning.
Beyond rubrics’ usage as reward, we repurpose rubrics to guide both online data selection and policy supervision. An LLM judge tags each rollout using a predefined rubric vocabulary shared across environments. The resulting profiles guide the selection of data that aligns with the overall behavioural composition of the mixed-environment batch while limiting overlap with already-selected data. Available positive rubrics (describing desired behaviours) provide privileged context for an on-policy self-distillation teacher, supplying additional token-level supervision, while negative rubrics (describing undesired behaviours) guide subsequent rollout generation away from recurring failure modes.
Together, these components form RISED . Across model backbones, RISED achieves the highest mean pass rate across environments and ranks first or second in every individual environment. Rubric-based analysis of RISED can further characterize the behavioural changes accompanying these gains.

Rubric-based analysis of RISED can further characterize the behavioural changes accompanying these gains. 1 Introduction Training a single LLM agent across diverse interactive environments offers a promising route toward generalist agents ( NVIDIA, 2025a ; Ren et al., 2026 ) . Joint training can benefit from transfer across environments and achieve performance comparable to separately trained specialists ( Zeng et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . We study joint training on mixed-environment batches, where multiple environments contribute to each policy update ( NVIDIA, 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Within a limited update budget, an important question is which prompt groups to select from the current rollouts to improve joint training. Existing approaches address different aspects of training-data allocation. Curriculum methods typically allocate training across domains or environments ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Zhu et al., 2026b ) , or adjust sample-level priorities using periodically refreshed difficulty estimates ( NVIDIA, 2025b ) . Online selection instead operates on current rollouts and can adapt to the evolving policy, but commonly prioritizes individual examples using local signals such as reward variability or estimated difficulty ( Jiang et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . Neither explicitly accounts for relationships between current rollouts from different environments. A second challenge arises from reward-based supervision. Under GRPO, identical rollout rewards provide no within-group reward contrast to distinguish which behaviours should be reinforced. In multi-environment training, all-failure and all-success groups can occur frequently because environments are learned at different rates. In our experiments, they constitute more than half of the candidate prompt groups, leaving substantial training data without a group-relative reward signal. Figure 1 : Overview of RISED . Sec. 2.2 describes the offline rubric discovery. Sec. 2.4 and Sec. 3 describe the selection and distillation, respectively. Together, these form RISED , which uses rubrics to select training data across diverse agentic environments and reuses them for on-policy self-distillation. Both challenges highlight limitations of relying solely on scalar reward signals in multi-environment RL. Reward-level statistics may be too coarse to characterize relationships relevant to cross-environment transfer, while identical rewards provide no within-group reward contrast. Recent work has explored textual feedback, such as rubric-based guidance, as richer supervision than scalar rewards and demonstrated its effectiveness for training LLMs and agents ( Gunjal et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . We find that rubric-based feedback is useful beyond policy supervision: it can serve as an effective online data-selection signal for capturing cross-environment relationships, while the same annotations can supply complementary supervision for groups with identical rewards ( Bablani et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . Concretely, an LLM judge tags each rollout using a shared, predefined rubric vocabulary (Sec. 2.2 ), producing rubric profiles that make rollout behaviours comparable across environments. We also investigate whether rubric profile similarity is informative about cross-environment transfer: our preliminary analysis finds that it correlates more strongly with cross-environment reward improvements than gradient similarity (Sec. 2.3 ). Motivated by this finding, we select prompt groups that align with the overall rubric profile of the mixed-environment batch while limiting overlap with already-selected groups (Sec. 2.4 ). Additionally, the same rubric information is reused during post-training. Available positive rubrics (describing desired behaviours) provide privileged context for an on-policy self-distillation teacher, yielding additional token-level supervision even when rollout rewards are identical, while negative rubrics (describing undesired behaviours) guide subsequent rollout generation away from recurring failure modes (Sec. 3 ). Together, these components form RISED : R ubr I cs for agentic multi-environment S election and s E lf- D istillation, with an overview of the framework in Fig. 1 . Across model backbones, RISED achieves the highest mean pass rate across environments, while component ablations demonstrate the complementary benefits of selection and self-distillation. Rubric-based analysis further reveals more frequent positive behaviours than in baseline rollouts, providing an interpretable account of the behavioural changes accompanying these gains. Our contributions are: • We adopt rollout-level rubric profiles as behavioural descriptions (Sec. 2.2 ) and empirically show that rubric similarity correlates more strongly than gradient similarity with cross-environment reward improvements (Sec. 2.3 ). • We propose RISED , a framework for multi-environment agentic RL that uses the same predefined rubric vocabulary across environments for online prompt-group selection and self-distillation. The selection component uses rubric profiles to select prompt groups across environments (Sec. 2.4 ). Positive rubrics condition the self-distillation teacher, while negative rubrics guide subsequent rollout generation (Sec. 3 ). • We conduct extensive experiments and ablations to evaluate RISED across multiple model backbones (Sec. 4.3 ) and demonstrate the complementary benefits of selection and self-distillation. We further use rubric profiles to characterize the behavioural changes accompanying these gains (Sec. 5 ). 2 Rubrics For Data Selection 2.1 Problem Setup We train a single policy jointly over a set of environments ℰ \mathcal{E} using GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . Prompts are scheduled for rollout generation in a round-robin manner across environments, targeting a uniform environment mixture, aligned with previous work setting ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . At each training step t t , we construct a candidate batch ℬ t \mathcal{B}_{t} of rollout groups. Each group g = ( τ g , i ) i = 1 n g=(\tau_{g,i})_{i=1}^{n} contains n n rollouts sharing a prompt x g x_{g} from environment e ⁡ ( g ) ∈ ℰ e(g)\in\mathcal{E} . A rollout τ g , i = ( x g , y g , i ) \tau_{g,i}=(x_{g},y_{g,i}) consists of the prompt and a completion or interaction sequence y g , i y_{g,i} generated by the rollout policy. We oversample by a factor of two, forming | ℬ t | = 2 ​ k |\mathcal{B}_{t}|=2k candidate groups ( 2 ​ k ​ n 2kn rollouts in total), and select a subset 𝒮 t ⊆ ℬ t \mathcal{S}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{B}_{t} of | 𝒮 t | = k |\mathcal{S}_{t}|=k groups ( k ​ n kn rollouts) for the policy update. Two properties of this setup are worth emphasizing. First, the choice is made online , once per step, against the current policy, unlike one-time selection of a fixed training subset, which cannot respond to a policy that keeps changing. Second, selecting from a 2 × 2\times candidate pool rather than the full task set bounds the cost: in RL, scoring a candidate usually requires generation, so evaluating the entire pool at every step is not affordable. Generating a surplus and selecting down is a standard compromise in online batch selection ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2015 ; Mindermann et al., 2022 ; Zou et al., 2026 ) , and similar patterns are seen in RL post-training ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) . 2.2 Rubric Construction From rubrics as rewards to rubrics as descriptions. Rubrics decompose rollout quality into individually identifiable behaviours and have primarily been used as reward signals for RL ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Jia et al., 2026 ; Rezaei et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . We repurpose these behavioural descriptions for sample selection, using shared rubric profiles to compare rollouts across environments. Using them as rewards requires careful calibration: every criterion is eventually folded into a scalar ( Tyagi et al., 2026 ) , so a missing or miscalibrated criterion can provide no gradient toward an omitted behaviour, or the wrong one. This requirement is expensive in agentic environments, where a task may admit many successful rollouts and exhaustively specifying in advance the desired good behaviours is difficult. We ask considerably less of the criteria: we identify the prominent behaviours exhibited by each rollout and compare rollouts through these behavioural profiles. 1 1 1 For selection, an incomplete rubric set may make rollouts appear more similar, weakening the signal rather than directly defining an incorrect reward. A more important requirement when using rubrics for selection is consistency across rollouts. The criteria need not exhaustively cover desirable behaviours, but should capture enough variation to distinguish rollouts. Rubric Vocabulary. Each rubric denotes a fine-grained behavioural pattern, represented by a snake_case name. We construct a predefined rubric vocabulary from warm-up model rollouts and augment it with behaviours identified in stronger LLM-generated rollouts. Because warm-up rollouts predominantly end in failure, successful LLM-generated rollouts are introduced to improve coverage of desired behaviours that would otherwise be underrepresented. Together, these sources broaden coverage of desired and undesired behaviours, described by positive and negative rubrics, respectively. We use Gemini-2.5-Pro to propose rubric names from warm-up rollout behaviours, consolidate semantically similar names, and organize them into skills. We then augment the vocabulary by extracting additional behaviours from teacher rollouts generated by Claude-Opus-4.6 and warm-up rollouts again, merging redundant names before incorporating new rubrics. The final vocabulary contains 82 rubrics across 11 skills 2 2 2 The vocabulary is constructed from warm-up and teacher rollouts across four environments. The main experiments use three of these environments; removing the rubrics and skill specific to the excluded environment yields 59 rubrics grouped into 10 skills. , covering both environment-general and environment-specific behaviours. Each rubric includes a short description for teacher conditioning and training-time rollout guidance (Sec. 3 ). Rubric Extraction. Given a rollout and the two-level vocabulary, an LLM judge identifies a set of ( skill , rubric , role , count ) (\text{skill},\text{rubric},\text{role},\text{count}) tuples from the predefined vocabulary. This gives rollouts from different environments a common behavioural representation while allowing the judge to navigate the vocabulary hierarchically rather than through a single flat list. The role indicates whether the behaviour is desirable ( demonstrate ) or undesirable ( violate ), while count records the number of occurrences of that behaviour identified in the rollout. Rubric extraction requires one judge inference call per rollout, without gradient computation. We serve Qwen3-32B locally and tag completed rollouts asynchronously, overlapping rubric annotation with rollout generation. App. C.6 reports the tagging overhead. The complete construction and extraction pipeline, including prompts and example rubric names, is provided in App. A . 2.3 Does Rubric Similarity Track Cross-Environment Transfer? Setup. We test whether similarity between rubric profiles is associated with cross-environment transfer. We train a policy on one source environment and evaluate it on both the source and held-out environments. We measure reward improvements in each environment to assess the benefits of source-environment training, with improvements on held-out environments indicating cross-environment transfer. A useful similarity signal should assign higher similarity to environments that exhibit larger reward improvements. We present results with WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) as the source environment in the main text and repeat the analysis with DBBench ( Liu et al., 2024 ) as the source in App. C.1 . For the WebShop setting, we evaluate on WebShop, DBBench, ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ) , and AppWorld ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ) , covering shopping, database interaction, household object manipulation, and application-based tasks, respectively. Detailed environment descriptions are provided in App. B.1 . Every 25 25 training steps up to step 500 500 , we freeze the policy and collect 512 512 fresh WebShop training rollouts ( 64 64 prompts × \times 8 8 samples), together with four rollouts per validation prompt from each environment. For this analysis, we use a fixed set of up to 200 validation prompts per environment across all checkpoints, retaining the full set when fewer than 200 are available. Each rollout is annotated with its corresponding rubrics. A stronger correlation indicates that a similarity signal more closely tracks which environments improve during WebShop training. As shown in Tab. 1 , the strongest positive correlations are obtained using the combined positive-and-negative rubric profile. Using both roles provides stronger positive associations, particularly on held-out environments, suggesting that similarities in both successful behaviours and failure modes are informative for cross-environment transfer analysis. Aggregating rubrics into broader skills generally weakens this signal. For example, WebShop and DBBench both contain rubrics belonging to the skill tool_usage_and_formatting . Skill-level aggregation therefore makes them appear similar even when the underlying fine-grained behaviours differ. Rubric similarity also consistently identifies which environment benefits most from training across all four environments: it identifies the most-improved environment at all 19 19 evaluated checkpoints, compared with 8 8 checkpoints for gradient similarity. Gradient signal is less strongly correlated with reward improvements in this analysis. Additionally, we evaluate the stability of the tagging procedure by independently re-tagging the same rollouts. Independent re-tagging yields similar environment-level transfer correlations, with the reported Spearman coefficients changing by at most 0.060 0.060 (App. C.2 ). 2.4 Rubrics for Online Data Selection The environment-level analysis motivates using fine-grained rubric counts from both positive and negative rubrics as a shared representation. A fixed vocabulary shared across environments makes these profiles directly comparable across environments and training steps. We now apply this representation to online prompt-group selection. Selection. A similar form is common in online batch selection for supervised fine-tuning ( Zou et al., 2026 ) and RL ( Lin et al., 2026 ) , though typically over embeddings rather than rubrics. Rubric-based selection therefore retains many groups whose identical rewards provide no within-group contrast to distinguish which behaviours should be reinforced. We then reuse the same rubric annotations for self-distillation to provide complementary token-level supervision on the selected rollouts. 3 Rubrics For Distillation On-policy self-distillation. Distillation trains a student to match a teacher’s output distribution rather than a hard label, providing a dense per-token target in place of a scalar reward. On-policy distillation applies this target to the student’s own rollouts, correcting the policy on states it actually visits ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . In self -distillation, teacher and student generally share parameters but differ in conditioning: the teacher is the same policy given privileged context c c unavailable to the student ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) . Thus, no separate teacher is trained, and supervision requires only an additional forward pass. The rubrics already tagged for batch selection also provide the privileged context c c , requiring no additional effort. For each rollout, we take the deduplicated union of its top- 3 3 ( 3 3 highest-count rubrics) positive rubrics and the top- 3 3 positive rubrics of its group, and render their descriptions as a privileged context for the teacher. Groups without positive rubrics may receive no rubric-derived teacher context (App. E.6 ). Distillation then trains the student to reproduce the desired behaviour without the privileged context c c . The choice to include only positive rubrics in the distillation context is motivated by prior work and supported by our ablation. Prior work similarly constructs rubric-conditioned teachers from the best rollouts ( Xia et al., 2026a ) or compress rollouts into separate contextual lessons ( Xia et al., 2026b ) . Mixing positive and negative material is not consistently beneficial, with its effect depending on the difficulty and comprehensibility of the context ( Armandpour et al., 2026 ) . Our ablation in App. C.3 likewise shows that filling context slots with both positive and negative rubrics degrades overall performance. Nevertheless, negative rubrics contain valuable information, particularly early in training. On ALFWorld, for example, negative-tagged rollouts outnumber positive-tagged rollouts by more than 10 × 10\times at step 10 10 , but fall below parity around step 330 330 . We use negative rubrics to steer the next step’s rollouts rather than to condition the teacher. At the end of each step, we aggregate tags over all candidate rollouts from each environment and compare the numbers containing at least one negative rubric and at least one positive rubric. If violations are more prevalent, we prepend that environment’s top- 3 3 negative rubrics to the next step that environment’s prompts as an “anti-patterns” block. When this steering is active, z z in Eq. 2 denotes the resulting steered prompt. The same z z is provided to both student and teacher, while only the positive-rubric context c c is privileged to the teacher. Overall, negative rubrics steer how rollouts are sampled, whereas positive rubrics provide the self-distillation target. Negative-rubric injection is used only during training. Validation rollouts use the original task prompts, without injected rubrics or privileged teacher context. Combining selection in Sec. 2.4 and the distillation here, we propose our approach RISED : R ubr I cs for agentic multi-environment S election and s E lf- D istillation, as the full algorithm summarized in Alg. 1 in Appendix. 4 Experiments and Results 4.1 Experimental Setting We build on AgentRL ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , which provides a unified function-call interface for multi-turn interaction. We train jointly on three AgentBench environments ( Liu et al., 2024 ) : ALFWorld, WebShop, and DBBench. The three differ in action space, reward mechanics, and rollout length, which is what makes their interaction non-trivial. An episode is capped at 20 20 interaction turns and 8192 8192 total tokens, and an unfinished episode receives − 0.2 -0.2 . We use GRPO with a batch of 64 64 prompts and n = 8 n=8 rollouts per prompt. At each step, the rollout buffer generates 128 128 prompt groups, from which we select 64 64 (Sec. 2.4 ). Across all runs, we follow the AgentRL training protocol, including environment-wise advantage normalization and stale-policy rollout generation. We evaluate validation pass rate every 10 10 training steps on fixed held-out sets, sampling 4 4 rollouts for each validation prompt. For each environment, we report the mean pass rate (binary success indicator) across prompts and rollouts. Overall performance is the unweighted mean of the three environment-level pass rates. To evaluate effectiveness across model backbones, we train Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (use Qwen2.5-3B later for simplicity) on four nodes with eight H100 GPUs each and Qwen3-4B without thinking on eight B200 GPUs. Methods requiring rubric annotations, including RISED , its component ablations, and distillation baselines, additionally use a dedicated eight-GPU server for Qwen3-32B judge inference. We report main results as the mean and standard deviation over multiple runs. Additional ablation experiments use a single seed unless otherwise stated. Full optimization and rollout hyperparameters are given in App. B . 4.2 Baselines We compare against five baselines. GRPO-64 uniformly samples 64 64 prompts and generates 8 8 rollouts per prompt, using all 512 512 rollouts per step without selection. GRPO-128 doubles the prompt batch size to 128 128 and updates on all 1024 1024 rollouts. Like RISED , Global Variance and Round-Robin Variance generate 128 128 candidate groups and select 64 64 for training based on within-group reward variance. Reward variance provides an inexpensive proxy for a GRPO learning signal: groups with identical rewards have zero variance. For binary rewards, variance induces the same ordering as mean absolute group-standardized advantage. This motivates our variance-based selectors and relates them to DAPO’s filtering of zero-variance groups ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . RL online selection methods prioritize training examples using reward variability or policy-dependent difficulty. DAPO filters zero-variance groups and replenishes the training batch ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , while VCRL combines variance-based filtering with replay ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) . To avoid generating rollouts for uninformative prompts, PCL and DOTS predict policy-dependent difficulty and favor intermediate-difficulty examples ( Gao et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2025 ) . InSight combines a reward-variance term with difficulty weighting and information gain from historical outcomes ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) . For binary rewards, success rates closer to 0.5 0.5 correspond to higher reward variance, connecting the intermediate-difficulty preference of PCL and DOTS to VCRL’s variance-based filtering and InSight’s variance component. These connections motivate our variance baselines as representative implementations of the shared preference for reward variability. We instantiate this principle using observed rollout rewards to select a fixed number of already-generated groups, matching RISED ’s candidate-generation budget and selection size. CROPI periodically selects training subsets using validation-guided influence estimates computed from off-policy rollouts and projected gradients ( Zhu et al., 2026a ) . Its reliance on validation data for selection places it outside our comparison protocol, which uses neither validation-guided scoring nor per-group gradient computation. RISED instead uses rubric profiles of current rollouts to jointly select prompt groups for coverage of the mixed-environment batch while limiting redundancy across environments. Further discussion of curriculum, rubrics and distillation appears in App. D . 7 Conclusion We introduced RISED , a rubric-guided framework that combines online data selection with self-distillation for multi-environment agent training. By representing rollouts through a predefined and shared vocabulary across environments, RISED selects groups that balance cross-environment relevance and behavioral diversity, while rubric-conditioned self-distillation provides dense supervision even for groups with zero variance in rewards. Across two model backbones on multiple agent environments, RISED consistently improves over competitive baselines and rubric-level analyses provide an interpretable view of how behaviors evolve during training. A limitation is that rubric tagging and teacher inference add overhead. Future work shall improve efficiency and scale to larger policies and more environments. References Agarwal et al. (2024) R. We take rollouts from one warmup training run with model Qwen-2.5-3B-instruct at step 100 100 and ask Gemini-2.5-pro for rubric names. The warmup model is trained on 4 environments, with details of training data as described in App. B.1 . The unique rubric names yield roughly 1,150 1{,}150 . These are embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and grouped by clustering on cosine distance (threshold 0.5 0.5 , average linkage) into about 194 194 clusters, each represented by its centroid-closest member. Skills are introduced afterwards. We present the resulting clusters to the judge in separate batches to keep the prompt within the context limit. For each batch, the judge assigns a canonical rubric name, merges clusters that describe the same behaviour, and groups the resulting rubrics under higher-level skill headings. Because the batches are processed independently, the same capability can be named twice, so a second clustering pass over skill-name embeddings (cosine distance threshold 0.5 0.5 ) merges the duplicates. Skills are therefore discovered from the rubrics rather than imposed on them. Overall, this yields an initial vocabulary of 59 59 rubrics across 11 11 skills on 4 environments. Because the initial vocabulary is extracted from rollouts of a weak warm-up policy, it provides substantially better coverage of failure modes than of successful behaviours. We therefore augment it using two sources for each environment: 100 100 warm-up rollouts from Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and 100 100 teacher rollouts generated by Claude-Opus-4.6 . The former primarily expose failure behaviours, whereas the latter provide successful behaviours that the weak policy rarely exhibits. Each rollout is processed twice by Gemini-2.5-pro : once using the current vocabulary as a closed taxonomy and once using free-form rubric extraction. We implement rubric tagging using an asynchronous primary path and a retry path. The primary prompt always contains the predefined vocabulary and successfully processes approximately 98% of rollouts. Both paths use a tagging template that prioritizes supplied rubric names but permits additional names for uncovered behaviours. Such discovered names are rare, accounting for less than 1% of emitted rubric names. To reduce retry overhead, the retry path uses a shorter candidate list refreshed every ten steps from frequently observed rubric names in the preceding ten steps; this list may include discovered names. These updates affect only the retry candidate list, not the vocabulary supplied to the primary path. Before constructing selection profiles, returned names are normalized and mapped to predefined rubric identifiers using edit-distance matching. Teacher conditioning and rollout guidance use the predefined descriptions. Appendix D Additional Literature Review Multi-environment agentic RL. Joint training with multiple environments has been found to have the potential of matching environment-specific specialists ( Cheng et al., 2025 ; Wang and Ammanabrolu, 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Cross-domain studies also report positive transfer between tasks: In a five-domain comparison, mixed RL achieves performance comparable to separately trained and merged models at lower total training cost ( Wang et al., 2026b ) . For interactive agents, Liu et al. (2026b) identify state information richness and planning complexity as important correlates of cross-domain generalization. Joint training on a mixture is therefore raising more and more attention. Training strategies include sequential domain stages ( NVIDIA, 2025a ; Ren et al., 2026 ) and joint optimization over mixed-environment batches ( NVIDIA, 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Nemotron-Cascade 2 orders stages to reduce interference, but notes that suitable orderings depend on the model’s learning dynamics and that capability drift remains ( Yang et al., 2026b ) . We follow the mixed-batch approach, holding environment proportions fixed. Curriculum and domain allocation. RL-related curriculum methods control sample difficulty, category or domain allocation, and environment membership. Nemotron 3 Nano schedules sample difficulty using checkpoint-based pass-rate estimates, which are refreshed when training progress plateaus ( NVIDIA, 2025b ) . Nemotron-Cascade 2 orders training stages to mitigate inter-domain interference ( Yang et al., 2026b ) . MoDoMoDo optimizes domain mixtures using predicted training outcomes from pilot runs ( Liang et al., 2025 ) . Online adaptive methods include SEC’s bandit-based category sampling ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , RuleReasoner’s reward-history-based domain reweighting ( Liu et al., 2026a ) , and TAC’s use of gradient alignment to select the domain supplying each training batch ( Yang et al., 2026a ) . These methods primarily determine category or domain allocation, stage ordering, or sample difficulty. Our focus is complementary: selecting prompt groups from current mixed-environment rollouts under a prescribed environment allocation, with selection accounting for both the batch’s behavioural composition and previously selected groups. Closest to our rubric profiles as selection reference, AES aggregates trajectory-derived abilities into environment profiles and selects environment subsets using coverage, redundancy, and gradient conflict ( Zhu et al., 2026b ) , but note that they select on environment level but not prompt groups level. In our AgentRL-based implementation ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , we fix the candidate environment mixture and RISED ’s round-robin selection schedule to focus on the problem of prompt-group selection. Directly applying domain schedulers or environment-subset selection would change our experimental setting. We acknowledge that jointly optimizing these decisions remains a parallel but important direction which we currently do not focus on. Global Variance nevertheless allows selected environment proportions to vary with observed reward variance, providing a comparison with adaptive batch composition within the fixed candidate pool. Rubrics as reward. Rubrics decompose response quality into interpretable criteria and provide reward supervision for open-ended generation ( Gunjal et al., 2026 ; Jia et al., 2026 ) , agentic tool use ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and image captioning ( Huang et al., 2026 ) . Later work improves both the criteria and their use in optimization: RLCER evolves rubric criteria during training ( Sheng et al., 2026 ) , POW3R adapts criterion weights according to rollout variation ( Tyagi et al., 2026 ) , and CriPO uses self-distillation and advantage correction to recover learning signals for unexplored or suppressed criteria ( Xia et al., 2026a ) . These methods primarily construct or adapt rubric-based rewards, while CriPO additionally improves optimization under those rewards through self-distillation and advantage correction. RISED retains environment-provided rewards and instead uses behavioural rubrics for prompt-group selection, teacher conditioning, and rollout guidance. Our focus is therefore how behavioural rubrics organize training data and provide auxiliary supervision, rather than how rubric scores construct the reward. On-policy distillation and its selective variants. Distillation trains a student to match a teacher’s output distribution, providing dense token-level supervision. On-policy distillation applies this supervision to student-generated rollouts, reducing the distribution mismatch of off-policy imitation ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . Recent on-policy self-distillation methods construct a teacher from the student model, conditioning it on privileged information or feedback to provide dense supervision on student-generated rollouts ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) . Li et al. (2026b) link successful distillation to teacher–student compatibility and additional teacher capabilities, with learning concentrated on shared high-probability tokens. Several variants refine supervision through uncertainty and disagreement ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , token teachability ( Wang et al., 2026c ) , trajectory filtering and token reweighting ( Li et al., 2026c ) , or trust-region restrictions on teacher supervision ( Xing et al., 2026 ) . For multi-turn agents, Skill-SD constructs teacher context from rollout-derived skill summaries and derives the importance-weighted reverse-KL objective ( Wang et al., 2026a ) ; SDAR uses token-level gating to stabilize joint RL and self-distillation ( Lu et al., 2026 ) , while SERL studies which environmental feedback to distill and where to apply it ( Li et al., 2026a ) . We adopt Skill-SD’s objective, but construct privileged context from a shared cross-environment rubric vocabulary whose annotations also guide prompt-group selection. Our contribution is to use a shared behavioural rubric vocabulary jointly for prompt-group selection and self-distillation. The component ablations (Sec. 5 ) show that combining the two yields the strongest overall performance, supporting their complementary roles. Token-selection rules and alternative distillation losses address complementary optimization choices. Closest to our distillation component, RuPI supplies rubric criteria, including positive and negative criteria, as privileged teacher context ( Bablani et al., 2026 ) . Our All-Rubric SD baseline adapts this approach to agentic RL by retaining GRPO and using rollout-derived rubrics. RISED differs by combining distillation with prompt-group selection, while assigning positive rubrics to teacher conditioning and negative rubrics to rollout guidance. Appendix E FAQ E.1 Why use a fixed rubric vocabulary? Our goal requires comparing rubric profiles across environments and training steps. Dynamic generation of free-form rubric assigns semantically equivalent behaviours different names and therefore requires repeated clustering or alignment before profiles can be compared. In preliminary experiments, clustering free-form annotations yielded between 25 and 44 skills across checkpoints, making comparisons across steps and environments difficult. The verification of each step’s new rubrics can also be difficult. A fixed vocabulary instead provides a stable coordinate system for online comparison. E.2 Will the warm-up process in building vocabulary introduce additional time cost? The warm-up run, taking only 1 / 10 1/10 steps of full training, introduces a one-time preprocessing cost that is amortized across subsequent training runs: 1. Reuse across backbones. The warm-up policy provides failure trajectories used to discover negative rubrics. Once constructed, the resulting vocabulary is reused across training runs and model backbones, so a separate warm-up run is not required for each backbone. 2. Reduced recurring overhead. A predefined vocabulary reduces online tagging to label selection. In contrast, free-form extraction would require repeated name alignment or clustering to reconcile semantically equivalent labels and preserve comparability across rollouts and training steps. 3. Offline use of larger models. Rubric consolidation and description generation are performed offline using a larger model, while online tagging uses a locally served judge. This avoids repeated large-model inference during training and reduces throughput overhead. E.3 Why evaluate rubric similarity at the environment level? We use environment-level analysis as a computationally tractable diagnostic of whether rubric similarity tracks reward improvements during single-environment training. Directly estimating the marginal benefit of individual prompt groups would require more expensive controlled updates and evaluations. The aggregate analysis motivates the predefined and shared rubric representation; it does not directly estimate each group’s contribution. We assess the practical utility of prompt-group selection through the main experiment and the end-to-end component ablations. E.4 Does reward-conditioned tagging affect the interpretation of rubric similarity? The judge receives rollout rewards and uses outcome-dependent instructions to identify desired and undesired behaviours. The resulting rubric profiles therefore reflect both behavioural content and outcome composition. The gradient baseline also incorporates rewards through its objective. Our comparison evaluates how well these two reward-informed representations track observed environment-level reward improvements. The stronger correlations support rubric similarity as an empirical diagnostic in this setting, but do not establish that its association is independent of reward composition. E.5 Are negative rubrics injected during validation? No. Negative rubrics guide training rollouts only. All reported validation results use the original task prompts without rubric injection. The role-filter ablation in App. C.3 and main results in Sec. 4.3 evaluate these training choices under the same unguided validation protocol. Its results show that the benefits of training-time guidance persist when the guidance is removed at evaluation. E.6 Does every group with identical rewards receive positive-rubric supervision? Not necessarily. Positive-rubric self-distillation can provide additional supervision for groups with identical rewards when positive rubrics are available within the group. Groups without positive rubrics lack this privileged behavioral context, and the distillation term has zero loss and gradients when teacher and student parameters and inputs coincide. However, negative rubrics can still provide a complementary mechanism by guiding subsequent rollout generation. E.7 Why not evaluate larger policy backbones? Agent RL is already computationally expensive at the 3–4B scale. For Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct , each run comprises 1000 1000 training steps on 32 32 H100 GPUs. Based on the measured average step times, even GRPO-64 requires approximately 1.8 1.8 days per run ( 155.5 155.5 s/step), while RISED requires approximately 2.9 2.9 days ( 252.9 252.9 s/step). Validation every 10 10 steps further increases the total runtime. Repeating training across baselines, ablations, and seeds incurs substantial computational cost. We therefore prioritize controlled comparisons across provided two backbones.
